evidence.claim: Follow the Okanogan River past towns once served by an earlier highway.
evidence.quote: In the original alignment, US 97 went straight north from Brewster on the west side of the Okanogan River, through the center of Okanogan, Omak, and Riverside before joining its current alignment.

evidence.claim: The Okanogan Trails Scenic Byway follows Highway 97 for 80 miles between the Canadian border and Pateros.
evidence.quote: Length 80 Miles | 128 KM Drive Time 2 Hours

evidence.claim: The Okanogan Trails Scenic Byway follows Highway 97 for 80 miles between the Canadian border and Pateros.
evidence.quote: Highway 97 between Pateros and the Canadian border

evidence.claim: State of Washington Tourism presents it as a drive through open landscapes and small towns, with history and outdoor recreation along the way.
evidence.quote: The Okanogan Trails Scenic Byway winds through the heart of North Central Washington, providing a mix of history, small-town charm, wide-open landscapes, and outdoor recreation.

evidence.claim: The tourism office gives the drive two hours; part of the route traces the western edge of the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation.
evidence.quote: Part of the route traces the western edge of the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation .

evidence.claim: The tourism office gives the drive two hours;
evidence.quote: Drive Time 2 Hours

evidence.claim: The road from Pateros to Okanogan entered the state system in 1905, and the extension to the Canadian border followed in 1907.
evidence.quote: In 1905, another road from Pateros to Okanogan was added to the system, which would be extended to the Canada–US border in 1907.

evidence.claim: It formed part of the Wenatchee-Oroville Road, numbered State Road 10.
evidence.quote: That roadway from Wenatchee to Canada, was named the Wenatchee-Oroville Road and numbered State Road 10.

evidence.claim: The US 97 number arrived in 1926, when the United States established its numbered highway system.
evidence.quote: The United States Numbered Highways were established in 1926 and US 97 was co-signed with all four state roads

evidence.claim: US 97 originally passed through central Okanogan, Omak and Riverside on the west side of the river.
evidence.quote: In the original alignment, US 97 went straight north from Brewster on the west side of the Okanogan River, through the center of Okanogan, Omak, and Riverside before joining its current alignment.

evidence.claim: A new alignment shifted traffic east of the river and bypassed Okanogan and Omak.
evidence.quote: The alignment shifted to a new highway on the east side of the river, bypassing Okanogan and Omak, which opened in 1964.

evidence.claim: Traveling south, begin beside Osoyoos Lake and pass through Oroville, then follow the river toward Tonasket.
evidence.quote: The highway continues north along the river to another crossing near the mouth of the Similkameen River south of Oroville. US 97 travels through Oroville and along the west side of Osoyoos Lake

evidence.claim: Between Tonasket and Riverside, the highway crosses the river and uses Wagonroad Coulee.
evidence.quote: following its west bank until the town of Riverside, where it splits to use Wagonroad Coulee. US 97 crosses the Okanogan River and follows its east bank into Tonasket

evidence.claim: Beyond the Omak and Okanogan bypasses, it rounds Soap Lake Mountain and reaches the Fort Okanogan area before Brewster.
evidence.quote: After a junction with SR 17 near the historic site of Fort Okanogan, US 97 turns north to follow the east bank of the Okanogan River in the Colville Indian Reservation. The highway travels along the river as it rounds Soap Lake Mountain

evidence.claim: Beyond the Omak and Okanogan bypasses, it rounds Soap Lake Mountain and reaches the Fort Okanogan area before Brewster.
evidence.quote: The highway continues northeast along the river to Brewster, where it intersects SR 173 before turning east towards Anderson Field. After a junction with SR 17 near the historic site of Fort Okanogan, US 97 turns north

evidence.claim: The drive ends at Pateros, where the Methow meets the Columbia.
evidence.quote: Pateros Located at the confluence of the Methow and Columbia rivers

evidence.claim: Oroville’s downtown includes historic buildings and public art.
evidence.quote: Oroville features historic buildings, local shops, eateries, and public art all downtown.

evidence.claim: In 1892 it became Oro, the Spanish word for gold, in an effort to attract prospectors and merchants.
evidence.quote: The settlement was named Oro, after the Spanish word for gold, in 1892 after the surrounding gold mines and in an attempt to attract prospectors and merchants.

evidence.claim: The Post Office objected because Washington already had an Oso, and Oro became Oroville in 1909.
evidence.quote: The Post Office objected to the name "Oro" because a town was already named "Oso" in Washington, so the name was changed to Oroville, in 1909.

evidence.claim: Rail connections changed too: a branch south to Wenatchee opened in 1914 to avoid the steep inclines of the original Spokane track.
evidence.quote: In 1914 a third branch south to Wenatchee was constructed to avoid the steep inclines on the original Spokane track.

evidence.claim: US 97 now runs through town at the south end of Osoyoos Lake, where the lake empties into the Okanogan River.
evidence.quote: It is located at the south end of Osoyoos Lake, which empties into the Okanogan River on the east side of the town; the town is bound to the west by the Similkameen River. U.S. Route 97 runs through Oroville.

evidence.claim: Great Northern passenger trains served Oroville until July 14, 1953; freight service continued afterward.
evidence.quote: Passenger train service to Oroville was operated by the Great Northern Railway until July 14, 1953, with freight operations continuing later.

evidence.claim: Downtown Omak has murals and preserved landmarks, while US 97 bypasses the city center.
evidence.quote: multiple murals and preserved landmarks located throughout the downtown area.

evidence.claim: while US 97 bypasses the city center.
evidence.quote: The highway also bypasses Omak

evidence.claim: The city operates a Main Street Historical Tour in its central business district.
evidence.quote: the City of Omak operates a Main Street Historical Tour in the central business district.

evidence.claim: Its Omak Stampede began in 1933 and takes place on the second weekend of August.
evidence.quote: The Omak Stampede, which operates the Suicide Race, has been hosted at a local rodeo facility, the Stampede Arena—renovated in 2009—since 1933. The Omak Stampede occurs annually on the second weekend of August.

evidence.claim: The event includes the Suicide Race, in which horses and riders descend a 62-degree slope to the Okanogan River.
evidence.quote: As part of the Suicide Race, horses and riders run down Suicide Hill—a 62-degree slope that runs for 225 feet (69 m) to the Okanogan River.

evidence.claim: Horses undergo veterinary examinations and a swim test; animal-welfare organizations have opposed the race over concerns for the horses.
evidence.quote: Horses must pass a veterinarian examination to ensure they are physically healthy, and a swim test to ensure they can cross the river, to demonstrate their ability to run the race and navigate the river. Several animal rights groups, including Progressive Animal Welfare Society (PAWS), In Defense of Animals and Humane Society of the United States (HSUS), have expressed concerns about the horses' welfare and have opposed the specific event.

evidence.claim: SR 215 provides local access through Omak and neighboring Okanogan, linking the bypass to the towns.
evidence.quote: US 97/SR 20 then intersects SR 215, which provides local access through Okanogan and Omak

evidence.claim: The original Fort Okanogan site lies beneath Lake Pateros, flooded in 1967 after construction of Wells Dam.
evidence.quote: The site of the fort was flooded in 1967 by the reservoir Lake Pateros, formed by construction of Wells Dam.

evidence.claim: John Jacob Astor’s Pacific Fur Company established the post in 1811 at the meeting of the Okanogan and Columbia rivers.
evidence.quote: Fort Okanogan (also spelled Fort Okanagan but only by nonresident Canadians) was founded in 1811 on the confluence of the Okanogan and Columbia Rivers as a fur trade outpost. Originally built for John Jacob Astor’s Pacific Fur Company

evidence.claim: The North West Company acquired it in 1813, and Hudson’s Bay Company took over after the companies merged in 1821.
evidence.quote: The North West Company, the PFC's primary competitor, purchased its assets and posts in 1813. In 1821 the North West Company was merged into Hudson's Bay Company

evidence.claim: The buildings had disappeared by 1880, well before the reservoir.
evidence.quote: No buildings of Fort Okanogan remained by 1880.

evidence.claim: The separate interpretive center became part of the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation’s History/Archaeology Program after the park transferred out of state ownership in 2011.
evidence.quote: Because of budget constraints, the park was transferred out of state ownership in 2011 to the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation. The FOIC is part of the Colville Tribes' History/Archaeology Program.
